claims.text: In BCC high-entropy alloy superconductors, Tc is primarily governed by the interplay of valence electron count and disorder-induced pair-breaking scattering.
Uranium contributes intermediate-valence f-electrons in the modified alloy.
Replacing Zr with U leaves the nominal valence electron count approximately constant.
Replacing Zr with U introduces additional pair-breaking scattering that suppresses Tc.
[TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69 has a BCC structure.
[TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69 is superconducting and has a large upper critical field.
The Zr-containing baseline exhibits phonon-mediated superconductivity in the weak electron-phonon-coupling regime.
The U-containing alloy retains a BCC structure.
U sites are stochastically distributed in the BCC high-entropy-alloy lattice.
U substitution increases local disorder and electron-scattering effects relative to Zr substitution.
The incorporated U does not contribute significant local magnetism under the specified conditions.
U-derived scattering centers reduce the effective electron-phonon coupling strength.
The additional scattering weakens Cooper pairing and suppresses superconductivity.
The U-containing alloy will have a lower Tc than the Zr-containing baseline.
The U-containing alloy will have a lower Hc2 than the Zr-containing baseline.
The superconducting properties of the Zr-containing baseline follow the expected valence-electron-count trend.
Localized U f-electrons and significant magnetic moments would place the system outside the proposed mechanism's boundary conditions.
Holding synthesis and processing conditions identical provides a controlled comparison between the Zr- and U-containing alloys.
Failure to observe statistically significant Tc suppression and a corresponding lower Hc2 in the U alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of increased disorder-induced pair-breaking would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The conditions restrict measurements to temperatures below the superconducting transition, whereas determining Tc by resistivity or susceptibility requires measurements spanning the transition, including temperatures above it.
